title: The Evening Brief: Defamation verdict, tariffs take effect, visa ban struck down
dek: The evening closes with a rare defamation loss for the New York Times, U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods now in effect with retaliation set for September 8, and a federal judge vacating the Trump administration's 75-country immigrant visa ban. Domestically, the Pentagon fired Stars and Stripes leadership over editorial independence, and Texas reduced a Sandy Hook judgment against Alex Jones. Internationally, Russia struck a Ukrainian shopping mall killing 16, Hong Kong activists await sentencing, and Nancy Kassebaum Baker, the first woman elected to the Senate in her own right, has died at 94.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Friday brought three major legal setbacks for the Trump administration: a defamation verdict against the Times on crime reporting, a federal judge's strike-down of the 75-country visa ban as violating immigration law, and a Supreme Court stay allowing ballroom construction, while tariffs on Canadian goods took effect and retaliation looms September 8.
bottom_line: The evening consolidated a day of legal strain on federal authority: a defamation verdict against the Times, a federal judge's strike-down of the visa ban as unlawful discrimination, and the opening of a tariff front with Canada effective immediately and Canadian retaliation set for September 8. Domestically, the Pentagon's firing of Stars and Stripes leadership on insubordination grounds frames an ongoing dispute over editorial independence within a government agency. Internationally, Hong Kong's convictions of democracy activists, Russia's continued strikes on Ukrainian civilians, and Israel's completion of settlement reversals mark ongoing pressure on democratic governance and territorial stability. The coming week will test whether the State Department appeals the visa ban ruling, whether the U.S. and Canada restart negotiations before September 8 retaliation, whether Stars and Stripes staff appeals succeed, and whether the Colorado River states reach a permanent agreement before October 19.
body: The evening closes a day marked by collision between federal authority and legal constraint. The New York Times sustained a $9.25 million defamation judgment to former Alabama basketball player Kai Spears, the first major loss on a published article in over 50 years, after the newspaper falsely reported he was present at a fatal 2023 shooting. The verdict exposes vulnerability for major news outlets when crime reporting involves false factual claims about an identified individual's presence at events. Separately, U.S. District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas struck down the Trump administration's policy suspending immigrant visas to 75 countries, ruling it violated the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, which prohibits discrimination based on nationality in visa issuance. Judge Vargas found the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio's legal authority and required reconsideration of visa denials made solely under the policy. The State Department announced the suspension in January 2026, stating it halted visas to citizens of Afghanistan, Brazil, Yemen and dozens of other countries because the administration determined people from those nations were likely to need public assistance. In a separate proceeding, Chief Justice John Roberts issued a temporary administrative stay allowing President Trump's $400 million White House ballroom construction to proceed, blocking lower court rulings that would have halted the above-ground portion of the project while litigation continues.

On trade, the United States imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian products effective 12:01 a.m. ET on August 22, 2026, hours before Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Canada would respond with matching retaliatory tariffs to take effect September 8. Trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed Friday night.

Domestically, the Pentagon dismissed Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, and Middle East correspondent Lara Korte on Friday, citing insubordination over unauthorized participation in a CBS Sunday Morning segment. Lederer's refusal to fire Slavin and Korte at Pentagon direction contributed to his own dismissal. Slavin stated in a statement to Fox News Digital that he was fired for saying in a CBS interview that censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line. The fired staffers were granted five days to appeal. The dismissals follow a Pentagon overhaul announced in January 2026 aimed at refocusing Stars and Stripes on military matters.

A Texas appellate court cut a $50 million judgment against Infowars founder Alex Jones to $1.5 million, finding Sandy Hook parents did not show evidence that harassment exceeded the state's damage cap. The unanimous Texas Third Court of Appeals opinion found that parents Neil Heslin and Scarlett Lewis failed to prove harassment rose to a level permitting them to exceed Texas's $750,000 per-plaintiff damages cap. A separate $1.4 billion Connecticut judgment against Jones remains unchanged.

International developments continued the day's pattern of legal constraint and military pressure. Two Russian drones struck a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine in a double-tap strike Friday, killing 16 people and injuring 130, with 4 remaining missing. The second drone targeted emergency workers already responding to the first strike. In Hong Kong, Lee Cheuk-yan, a 69-year-old lawmaker, and Chow Hang-tung, a 41-year-old lawyer, were convicted of inciting others to subvert state power under the national security law for their roles as leaders of the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance, which organized annual vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown. Both face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison, with sentencing expected at a later date. A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, pleaded guilty in January. Human rights groups have designated the defendants as prisoners of conscience. Israel reestablished the Kadim settlement in the occupied West Bank with 30 families, reversing a 2005 evacuation and completing the reopening of all four settlements dismantled two decades ago as part of the Disengagement Plan.

Federal enforcement actions earlier in the day secured a $400 million settlement with TikTok and ByteDance resolving litigation over alleged violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. TikTok will pay $300 million immediately, with an additional $100 million contingent on vacating a prior consent decree related to Musical.ly. The Interior Department mandated a reduction of 1.25 million acre-feet of Colorado River water annually for two years beginning in 2027 for California, Nevada, and Arizona, with Arizona bearing the largest cut at 760,000 acre-feet, California 440,000 acre-feet, and Nevada 50,000 acre-feet. The department warned it could order additional cuts over the next 10 years.

On the legislative side, California State Sen. Aisha Wahab won the special election for the state's 14th House District, defeating fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez 53% to 47% with 95% of votes counted. Wahab will serve the remainder of former Rep. Eric Swalwell's term. Swalwell resigned from Congress in April amid allegations of sexual assault, which he has denied. Federal Judge Nusrat Choudhury ruled that former Abercrombie & Fitch CEO Mike Jeffries is competent to stand trial on sex trafficking charges, reversing an earlier finding of mental incompetence based on examination of medical records and over 21 hours of audio recordings across 109 calls. Trial is scheduled to begin October 26. Laken Snelling, 22, a former University of Kentucky STUNT team member, pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter in the death of her newborn son, whose body was found wrapped in a towel inside a trash bag in a closet. She faces up to 10 years in prison, with sentencing set for October 16, 2026.

Nancy Kassebaum Baker, the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without following a spouse into office, died at 94 of natural causes. She represented Kansas from 1978 to 1997, serving three terms. She was the only female committee chair among eight women senators when she retired in 1996. She later endorsed Democratic candidates and called for President Trump's impeachment following the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack.
